topics.summary: What 3 x 4 really means, and why it is not 3 + 4.

topics.name: Equal Parts

objectives.text: Say what a multiplication like 4 x 5 means.
Write a multiplication for a picture of equal groups.
Tell a multiplication problem from an addition problem.

keyTerms.definition: Groups that all have the same number of things in them.
To find how many altogether when you have equal groups.
The word we say for the x sign. 4 x 5 is read "four times five".

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body:
Multiplication is about EQUAL GROUPS.

You will learn what 4 x 5 really means.

You will learn how to tell when a problem needs multiplying.

sections.heading: Equal groups
sections.body:
Look at these four baskets. Each basket has 5 mangoes.

    [5]  [5]  [5]  [5]

How many mangoes altogether?

You could add:  5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20

That works. But writing 5 four times is slow. And with twenty baskets it would be very slow.

So we write it a shorter way:

    4 x 5 = 20

Read it as "four groups of five".

The 4 is how many groups. The 5 is how many in each group.

sections.heading: The groups must be EQUAL
sections.body:
This only works if every group is the same size.

Look at these baskets:

    [5]  [3]  [5]  [6]

You cannot write a multiplication for this. The groups are not equal.

Here you have to add: 5 + 3 + 5 + 6 = 19.

Multiplication is a shortcut, but it is only a shortcut for EQUAL groups. If the groups are different sizes, the shortcut does not work.
sections.example:
A word problem.

"A farmer plants 6 rows of maize. Each row has 8 plants. How many plants altogether?"

Ask yourself: are there equal groups?

Yes. There are 6 rows, and every row has the same number: 8.

So it is multiplication:

    6 x 8 = 48

There are 48 plants.

Now a different problem.

"A farmer plants 6 plants on Monday and 8 plants on Tuesday. How many altogether?"

Are these equal groups? No. One day is 6, the other is 8. They are just two amounts.

So this is addition:

    6 + 8 = 14

Same two numbers. Completely different answer. The words tell you which one to use.

sections.heading: Turning it around
sections.body:
Here is something useful.

    3 x 4 = 12
    4 x 3 = 12

The answer is the same both ways.

Why? Picture it.

    3 rows of 4:        4 rows of 3:
      * * * *              * * *
      * * * *              * * *
      * * * *              * * *
                           * * *

Both have 12 stars. It is the same stars, just turned.

This helps you. If you know 2 x 9, then you also know 9 x 2 — and 2 x 9 is much easier to work out.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. There are 5 bags. Each bag has 3 oranges. Write the multiplication and the answer.

2. What does 7 x 2 mean? Say it in words.

3. A shop has 4 shelves. Each shelf has 6 tins. How many tins?

4. Musu has 4 sweets. Her brother has 7 sweets. Is this multiplication or addition? Why?

5. If 8 x 3 = 24, what is 3 x 8? How do you know without working it out?

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Multiplication means equal groups.
• 4 x 5 means four groups of five.
• The groups must all be the same size, or you must add instead.
• Read the words carefully: equal groups means multiply, two different amounts means add.
• You can turn a multiplication around and the answer stays the same.

objectives.text: Say why parts must be equal to be halves, thirds or quarters.
Name the fraction when a whole is split into equal parts.
Say which is bigger, a half or a quarter, and why.

keyTerms.definition: One complete thing before you cut it up.
Pieces that are exactly the same size as each other.
One of two equal parts of a whole.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body:
A fraction is a part of one whole thing.

You will learn what halves, thirds and quarters are.

Most of all you will learn one word: EQUAL.

sections.heading: Equal is the whole idea
sections.body:
Two children share one loaf of bread.

One child cuts it like this:

    |=======|==|
      big     small

Is that fair? No.

Are those two pieces halves? NO.

Cutting something into two pieces does not make halves. The two pieces must be the SAME SIZE.

    |=====|=====|
      same   same

Now they are halves.

This is the mistake almost everyone makes at first. Remember it: two pieces is not enough. Two EQUAL pieces.

sections.heading: Naming the parts
sections.body:
The name depends on how many equal parts you make.

    Cut a whole into 2 equal parts → each part is a HALF
    Cut a whole into 3 equal parts → each part is a THIRD
    Cut a whole into 4 equal parts → each part is a QUARTER

We write them like this:

    one half     = 1/2
    one third    = 1/3
    one quarter  = 1/4

The bottom number tells you how many equal parts the whole was cut into.

The top number tells you how many of those parts you have.

So 3/4 means: the whole was cut into 4 equal parts, and you have 3 of them.
sections.example:
Sharing a cassava.

Three children share one cassava equally.

How many equal parts? Three.

So each child gets one third. We write it 1/3.

Now four children share one cassava equally.

How many equal parts? Four.

Each child gets one quarter, 1/4.

Here is the important question. Which child gets more — one of the three, or one of the four?

The same cassava was shared among MORE children the second time. So each piece must be smaller.

1/3 is bigger than 1/4.

More people sharing, smaller pieces. That is true every time.

sections.heading: More parts means smaller parts
sections.body:
This surprises people, so look at it carefully.

4 is a bigger number than 2.

But 1/4 is SMALLER than 1/2.

Why? Because the bottom number is not counting how much you have. It is counting how many ways the whole was split.

Split a mango between 2 people — big pieces.

Split the same mango between 4 people — small pieces.

Split it between 8 people — very small pieces.

The bigger the bottom number, the more people are sharing, and the smaller each share becomes.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. A cake is cut into 2 pieces, but one piece is much bigger. Are these halves? Why not?

2. A bread is cut into 4 equal parts. What is each part called?

3. Write "one third" using numbers.

4. What does 3/4 mean? Say it in words.

5. Which is bigger, 1/2 or 1/4? Explain why, using sharing.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• A fraction is a part of one whole.
• The parts must be EQUAL, or they have no fraction name.
• 2 equal parts are halves, 3 are thirds, 4 are quarters.
• The bottom number says how many equal parts the whole was cut into.
• The more parts, the smaller each part is.

questions.question: There are 5 bags. Each bag has 3 oranges. How many oranges altogether?
questions.explanation: These are equal groups — every bag has the same number. So multiply: 5 groups of 3 is 5 x 3 = 15. If you chose 8, you added 5 + 3 instead. Adding would only be right if the bags held different amounts.

questions.question: A farmer plants 6 rows of maize with 8 plants in each row. How many plants?
questions.explanation: Every row has the same number, so these are equal groups: 6 x 8 = 48. If you chose 14, you added 6 + 8. Look for the words "each row" — they tell you the groups are equal, so you multiply.

questions.question: If 8 x 3 = 24, what is 3 x 8?
options: You must work it out again
questions.explanation: It is 24 as well. Turning a multiplication around does not change the answer — 3 rows of 8 has exactly the same number of things as 8 rows of 3, just turned. This is worth remembering, because one way round is often easier to work out.

questions.question: A bread is cut into 2 pieces, but one piece is much bigger. Are these halves?
options: No, because halves must be equal in size
Yes, because all cuts make halves
Only the big piece is a half
questions.explanation: Cutting into two pieces is not enough. For them to be halves, the two pieces must be exactly the SAME SIZE. This is the mistake nearly everyone makes at first, so it is worth saying to yourself every time: two EQUAL pieces.

questions.question: A cassava is cut into 4 equal parts. What is each part called?
questions.explanation: Four equal parts means each one is a quarter, written 1/4. Two equal parts would be halves and three would be thirds. The number of equal parts gives the name.

questions.question: Which is bigger, 1/2 or 1/4?
questions.explanation: Think about sharing one mango. Between 2 people, the pieces are big. Between 4 people, the same mango gives smaller pieces. So 1/2 is bigger. The bottom number counts how many ways the whole was split, not how much you get — more parts means smaller parts.
